analysis.one_liner: Eliminates federal requirements that government construction contractors pay locally prevailing wages.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in April 2026 with a single cosponsor and has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee since, with no hearing or vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The Davis-Bacon Act requires companies on federally funded construction projects to pay workers at least the wage rate common for their trade and area — typically the union-scale rate. This bill repeals those wage requirements 30 days after enactment, leaving existing contracts and bids already outstanding untouched [S2]. If passed, contractors on federal projects could pay whatever the market's low end allows, cutting labor costs but also cutting construction workers' paychecks.
analysis.who_benefits: Construction contractors and developers bidding on federally funded projects gain the most: labor is the biggest cost in construction, and the prevailing-wage floor is often the difference between paying union-scale and paying the area's lowest rate. Firms that rely on lower-wage, nonunion labor would be able to underbid firms that pay full prevailing wages.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals subchapter IV of chapter 31 of title 40, U.S. Code — the Davis-Bacon wage requirements — and voids any other legal references to them, so no federal contract would carry a prevailing-wage obligation after the 30-day effective date [S2].
It grandfathers contracts already in existence and bids already solicited on the effective date, so current obligations are unaffected [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Construction workers on federally funded projects — laborers, electricians, plumbers, and equipment operators — would bear the cost, since the prevailing-wage floor that guarantees locally common pay and fringe benefits disappears. Union building trades would lose the wage standard that keeps lower-wage competitors from underbidding them with public money.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the prevailing-wage floor removes the guarantee that workers on federal construction earn the rate common for their trade and locality, which would pull pay on government-funded projects toward the area's lowest rate [S2].

The bill is written as a blanket repeal — it does not replace Davis-Bacon with any alternative wage standard or modernized wage-determination process, so the entire prevailing-wage regime ends rather than being reformed [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Repeal would lower the government's construction bills, and supporters argue prevailing-wage rules inflate bid costs and rely on wage determinations that can be out of date. But those savings come directly out of the paychecks of workers on federal projects, and lower bids often reflect a lower-skilled, lower-wage crew rather than genuine efficiency. The savings to taxpayers are real but modest in most analyses; the wage cut for affected workers is direct. On balance, the transfer runs from construction workers to contractors.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 30, 2026, and referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the same day; the committee has taken no further action on it since [S4].

narrative.text: Rep. Eric Burlison introduced the bill on April 30, 2026, for himself and Rep. Barry Moore of Alabama [S2].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Education and Workforce on the day of introduction and has had no other action recorded since [S4].
It has exactly one cosponsor, Rep. Barry Moore [S3].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything — the bill has not moved. If it stays dormant, the prevailing-wage protections it targets remain in place, which leaves federal construction contractors and the House sponsor without the change they sought, while construction workers keep the current wage floor.

for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Davis-Bacon wage requirements and referred it to the Education and Workforce Committee

against.what_they_did: Took no action after the April 30, 2026 referral — no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and its one cosponsor are both Republicans; only 1 of 223 House Republicans signed on and no Democrat did, so the bill is a single-party effort with almost no support even from the sponsor's own caucus [S3].

industries.industry: Construction contractors and developers on federal projects
industries.note: Repeal lets these firms cut the largest line item on federal jobs — labor — by paying below the local prevailing rate. The savings come out of their workers' paychecks.

industries.industry: Union building trades and union-signatory contractors
industries.note: Davis-Bacon's union-scale benchmark protects union wage standards on public work. Repeal would let low-wage nonunion crews underbid them on federally funded projects.

They could more easily win federal work at prevailing rates today; without the floor, they could still win the work but at lower pay. The bill removes the protection that currently sets their minimum.

analysis.trajectory: With one cosponsor, no committee action two weeks after referral, and no sign of a hearing, this bill follows the typical path of a solo-party labor repeal: it will likely sit in the Education and Workforce Committee and expire when this Congress ends in January 2027.
